View image in fullscreen
A person using an electric fan to cool down on the underground in London. Education, health services and transport all suffered in the heat. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA


Summer of 2026 was UK’s hottest on record, Met Office says


Meteorologists say mean average temperature of 16.5C was made 130 times more likely by climate crisis




This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data, and the Met Office said the season’s mean temperature was made 130 times more likely by the climate crisis.
Record-breaking and back-to-back heatwaves have scorched much of Europe. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels.

The Met Office said an average mean UK temperature of 16.5C made this summer provisionally the warmest on record as well as the warmest season in a series going back to 1884. England, Wales and Northern Ireland broke their respective mean temperature records for summer while Scotland recorded its joint sixth hottest summer.


This is the second year in a row that temperature records have been broken, with 2025 and 2026 both the warmest UK summers since records began.
The infamous summer of 1976 is now the seventh warmest on record in terms of mean temperature.
Katie White, the minister for climate transition, said it was a “brutal reminder that we’re not waiting for climate change to arrive in Britain, we’re living in the middle of it. With kids too hot to sleep, families worrying about older relatives, farmers watching fields dry out, and firefighters and our armed forces battling wildfires, we’ve all woken up to a reality none of us wants for the people and places we love.”


View image in fullscreen
Smoke rising from a major wildfire at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston, in late July.  Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA


England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone.
A study conducted by Met Office scientists showed this summer’s record-breaking heat was made about 130 times more likely because of human-induced climate change. The Met Office’s climate projections indicate that UK summers will continue to become hotter.
The Met Office’s head of climate attribution, Dr Mark McCarthy, said: “The summer of 2026 has been remarkable and is an example of the extremes we can expect to see more frequently as a consequence of human-induced climate change.”

articles.jina_text:
Andy Burnham has pledged to “meet the climate challenge” as he confirmed he would attend the annual UN climate summit in November.




Addressing MPs for the first time as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham said he would attend the Cop 31 meeting in Antalya, on Turkey’s southern coast, as his predecessors had done.








Pointing to last week’s devastating floods in Nepal, he told MPs: “This is what the climate crisis looks like.




“We have just ourselves experienced what is likely to have been the hottest summer on record.




“This Government will meet the climate challenge, and I can confirm to the House that I will attend Cop 31 in Turkey in November.”








His commitment to attend Cop 31 came only a few hours after provisional figures from the Met Office suggested 2026 was the UK’s hottest summer since records began.




The average temperature across June, July and August was 16.5C, beating the previous high of 16.1C set only last year.




This summer was also the first to see three separate days where temperatures exceeded 37C as parts of the country suffered as many as five heatwaves thought to have caused thousands of deaths.











Green Party MP Adrian Ramsey said the summer’s high temperatures required “a response that meets the needs of the moment and our future”, urging Mr Burnham not to approve new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.

The Met Office has confirmed the UK has provisionally experienced its hottest summer since records began nearly 150 years ago. 
Five heatwaves between May and August left the majority of the country in drought and have sparked wildfires and travel disruption.
The UK recorded a mean average temperature across June, July and August of 16.5C, beating the previous seasonal high of 16.1C set last year, the Met Office said. 





The forecaster previously suggested the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record, provided temperatures remained around average for the rest of August, and it is expected the final figures for the month will break the previous record.
Despite a cooler end to August, areas of high pressure have dominated, with dry conditions from continental Europe causing temperatures to rise.

The first heatwave in May also broke that month’s temperature record by more than 2C, while parts of the UK experienced a three-week heatwave in July and August.

SPONSORED BY OCTOPUS ENERGY

The Independent Home Channel is powered by Octopus Energy.
Solar panels can cut the amount of electricity you need to buy from the grid and give you more control over how your home uses energy. But getting the most from them involves more than simply choosing a set of panels and putting them on the roof.
Everything from the amount of shade your roof receives to when you use electricity – and what happens to the power you don’t use – can affect how well a solar installation works for your household. Batteries and smart energy tariffs can make a difference too.
If you’re thinking about going solar, keep reading to discover the seven things worth knowing before the installers arrive.

1. Shade matters more than you expect
A bit of light research into solar installation will inform you about the importance of roof orientation and pitch, but one area that doesn’t always come up is shade – and even partial shading can affect how much electricity you generate at certain times of day.
Trees, chimneys, neighbouring buildings and even roof features can reduce output during specific hours. A good installer will assess shading properly before you commit, so it’s worth making sure this forms part of your initial survey rather than assuming ideal conditions. Octopus Energy will assess levels of shading, then recommend the right tech for the job. For shadier roofs, for example, optimised microinverters can be fitted, which move the power conversion from a single central point to the individual panel level, allowing each panel to work independently of the others, maximising energy production.

2. A home battery can help you use more of your solar energy
One of the biggest surprises for new solar owners is how much electricity they generate when they’re not at home. If everyone’s out during the day, much of that power is exported back to the grid. A home battery helps make the most of this surplus by storing energy so it can be used later: in the evening, overnight, or during peak periods. With a smart import and export tariff, a battery can also be charged from the grid when electricity is cheaper, while surplus stored energy can potentially be exported when rates are higher.
Even if a battery isn’t installed straight away, thinking about it early can help future-proof your setup. Choosing compatible equipment, inverters and tariffs can make upgrades far simpler, particularly as electric vehicles, heat pumps and flexible energy pricing become more common.

Texas and Louisiana are bracing for Tropical Storm Edouard, which is expected to make landfall Tuesday.
​The storm, which has strengthened while heading towards the Texas Gulf Coast, threatens to bring with it heavy rain that could lead to flash flooding.
Early Tuesday the storm was about 65 miles south-southeast of Cameron, Louisiana, and 90 miles southeast of Port Arthur, Texas, with maximum sustained winds of 40 mph while moving west-northwest at 8 mph.





The National Hurricane Center warned the storm could approach hurricane strength before reaching the northwest Gulf Coast. 
“The biggest problem we expect with the storm at this moment in time is flooding,” Texas Governor Greg Abbott said at a Monday press conference. “Some local rainfall may be as high as 10-15 inches. Some could be 3 or 4 inches per hour.”

Almost 90 years ago this week Britain had basked in a glorious summer that was brought to a sudden and dramatic end by the declaration of war against Germany. Andy Burnham faces something similar, if less violent, as MPs return to Westminster for the first time since his “coronation”.



In 1939 many people wrongly believed hostilities would be over by Christmas. If Burnham does not get these next few months right, his hopes of being more than a one-term prime minister could really be over by the time we are tucking into the turkey.



He has got off to a flying start, bringing an energy and enthusiasm that cautious Keir Starmer never managed. Pledges to cut energy bills, bus fares and pub taxes, end homelessness, block vape and betting shops and arm Ukraine have all been well received. But after this flying start gravity is starting to reassert itself.

He has got off to a flying start, bringing an energy and enthusiasm that cautious Keir Starmer never managed. Pledges to cut energy bills, bus fares and pub taxes, end homelessness, block vape and betting shops and arm Ukraine have all been well received. But after this flying start gravity is starting to reassert itself.

 
There have been accusations of U-turns on political donations, council house building and the Elgin marbles along with reports of delays to the decision on both North Sea oil and gas drilling and welfare reform. If he is not careful that could start to add up to an all too familiar story. 
The VAT cut on energy bills has been eclipsed by an increase in the price cap. Making it one of his first acts, to try to give people ‘breathing space’, may buy him some credit. The danger is that voters feel gaslighted to see bills rise after he pledged to act. That is why we discussed the move more than once while I was in 10 Downing Street but never did it. Most polling shows an electorate short on patience and sick of being promised action on the cost of living that does not translate to better living standards. 
Then there is his decision to intervene over prisoner releases. The PM undoubtedly speaks for the public when he says he finds the early release scheme unacceptable. But the truth is that, unless something has drastically changed since my time in government, there simply are not enough jail places or any way of suddenly creating some. (My bright idea of tents behind barbed wire in the woods was repeatedly rejected over the risk of escapes.) 
Former Tory cabinet minister David Gauke’s review was intended to take the politics out of the issue as far as was humanly possible and point to the appalling inheritance the government received. Burnham’s changes means the killers of PC Andrew Harper will stay behind bars but there will always be hugely difficult edge cases. And many Labour MPs are deeply unhappy that offenders who have committed domestic violence will walk free early.



 
There is also disquiet in the Labour ranks over devolution plans, particularly among Scottish and Welsh MPs who wonder where they will be left if even more powers are given away to the devolved governments. 
This is the backdrop to Parliament’s return.

articles.jina_text:
For millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying.
The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action.

As the death toll continues to mount – the latest count showed more than 900 dead and more than 4,400 individuals missing – this event has crystalized the climate crisis for many.
One reason is undoubtedly the sheer horror of what unfolded here. Chilling surveillance and eyewitness footage captured the horrific moment a 40mph wall of “liquid concrete” violently overtook fleeing crowds, instantly swallowing entire families and burying them beneath feet of thick, red-soaked silt. Another reason, however, is that the connection with climate change was unassailable in this case.






The Nepal floods seem a world away – but make no mistake, climate breakdown will affect us all
Nesrine Malik


Read more
The torrent was the direct result of warming-induced glacial collapse, which dumped millions of tons of rock, unleashing a high-velocity wave of mud and debris. The new reality in the era of human-caused climate change, a CNN headline put it, is that “living downstream from a glacier has become a deadly liability”.
The impact of climate change on extreme weather, by contrast, is usually established though a statistical, rather than direct causal, connection. Through what is known as attribution science, climate scientists demonstrate the influence of climate change on the characteristics of an extreme weather event. It is analogous to how epidemiologists establish a linkage between cause (eg smoking cigarettes) and effect (lung cancer), through massive statistical evidence.
In the case of climate attribution, scientists run parallel climate model simulations, including a “control” simulation that represents a counterfactual world without human impact, and a “treatment” simulation where human drivers – primarily the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations – are included. They then compare how often a particular event happens in the two cases. If there is a substantial increase in occurrence of a particular event in the “treatment” simulation relative to the “control” simulation, then the extremeness of the event – and its human, societal or environmental impacts – can be “attributed” to climate change.

‘The mountains are changing’: What the floods tell us about the future of India’s Himalayas


As families await news of missing loved ones, the disaster is a stark reminder of how the climate crisis is creating a fast-growing threat. Plus, the town considered India’s ‘Jurassic Park’ 
 Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here




It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.

Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?

Cities sweltering and the smell of the middle ages: has the climate crisis killed Instagram’s Euro summer?

Brigid Delaney






Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven?





This week the Euro summer comes to an end – and so does a certain type of posting on Instagram.
Waiting at the bus stop in the grey winter dawn, a slanting rain soaking your trouser leg, you can warm yourself by scrolling your feed and seeing pictures of Australians enjoying a Euro summer. There it is again – azure Greek coves, plates of barbecued sardines, the yachts rented by the hour, and selfies on the balcony of some Paris Airbnb, drinking wine in the long, blue night.

But this year, just out of the frame but never far away, was the heat. You can’t easily photograph heat but it infused the season so monumentally that it might just have killed the Euro summer dream cold.
With extreme heat starting in late May, this summer broke temperature records in western Europe and made for an uncomfortable travel experience for hundreds of millions of tourists.







France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing land

Read more
Who dreams of having a Euro summer now when staying in an ancient, uncooled building in the Old Town is like trying to sleep in a wood-fired pizza oven? How aspirational and glamorous is it to spend your days in an air-conditioned shopping centre (if you can find one) because to try to see a cathedral or historic site is to risk heatstroke?
To travel to the usual European vacation spots in high season now is to endure. It’s to plan your travel so that you aren’t outside in the middle of the day. It’s to stay in places that have air conditioning – if you can find them – and pay a premium to try to stay cool.
It’s major monuments and attractions being closed because it’s too dangerous for them to remain open. (In June, Notre-Dame Cathedral restricted access to its towers, while the Eiffel Tower, which is normally open late, announced a 4pm closure, as did the Louvre.)


It’s the cities sweltering, smelling of the middle ages – decomposing rubbish, sweat and hot bodies. It’s the feeling of being drained of energy, jet-lagged and damp, lying on a hard mattress in your shuttered hotel room, face close to the fan, as the thick air turns.

articles.jina_text:
Flash flooding in Arizona tourist destination was likely triggered by compounding climate factors, such as drought and warming in Pacific Ocean 
 
 
Remote Grand Canyon lodge hit by deadly flash flood boasts fabled history 











A deadly flash flood in the Grand Canyon over the weekend was likely driven by a confluence of climate factors, including drought, wildfire scarring and warming temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that can supercharge storms.
At least two people have died, nearly 80 people were rescued and one remained unaccounted for after a surge of water and debris swept through the immensely popular tourist destination on Saturday, fueled by torrents of rain that hit the national park’s Bright Angel Creek area.




 
 
Flash floods are not uncommon in the region, especially during the monsoon season from June to September, when strong rains pummel the arid landscapes and can quickly fill narrow rock formations. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding, when clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly, transforming downpours into a charging wall of water.


View image in fullscreen
This handout image released by the National Park Service shows a storm system moving across the North Rim of Grand Canyon national park on 29 August. Photograph: J Baird/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images
But Saturday’s strong storm also hit part of the burn scar of the Dragon Bravo wildfire, a destructive and fast-moving blaze that swept across nearly 150,000 acres (60,700 hectares) and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge in July 2025.
Runoff tends to flow more quickly in the aftermath of a fire, especially in hotter burns where slopes are left barren of vegetation.
While it’s still unclear how directly long-term damage to the landscape from that fire played a role in last weekend’s disaster, federal models indicated a rise in the risks of debris flows in Bright Angel Creek.





Floods sweeping through Grand Canyon national park
Teams with the Department of Interior charged to assess post-fire threats to “life, property, and critical natural and cultural resources”, found runoff risks would be between two and eight times greater upstream of Phantom Creek. “Hikers on the trails within or downslope from the burned area will experience frequent stabilization issues, especially hazardous rockfall for at least the first year,” the team wrote in a report on conditions.
Park officials were reportedly concerned at the start of this summer that stronger storms could create dangerous conditions near the burned areas. Hikers that had to be evacuated by helicopter after the rushing waters swallowed bridges and other infrastructure told the Arizona Republic that the creek turned black as it filled with runoff.

Two people dead and nearly 80 rescued after Grand Canyon flash flood


Officials say one person still unaccounted for as forecast heavy rain and thunderstorms threaten further flooding




A second death was confirmed by National Park Service officials on Monday after a flash flood sent a surge of water and debris through an area of the Grand Canyon over the weekend.
Dozens of visitors had to be evacuated by helicopter during the deluge, which consumed trails and infrastructure. Nearly 80 people were rescued and one person is still unaccounted for, as more heavy rain and thunderstorms in the forecasts threaten additional debris flows, flash floods or rock falls, the NPS said in a statement.

“With deep monsoonal moisture in place and already saturated soils in some locations, an elevated risk of flash flooding will be in place through Monday,” the National Weather Service (NWS) said.
Incident commander Dave Black said officials used night-vision and other equipment to find people who needed to be evacuated over the weekend.

Park officials called on the public to provide any information on those who may have been hiking or backpacking in the inner canyon near Bright Angel Creek, or campers with a reservation in the area.


Flash floods are not uncommon in the region, especially during the monsoon season from June to September when strong rains pummel the arid landscapes and can quickly fill narrow rock formations. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, when clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
The deluge that unleashed torrents of rain on hardened and sparsely vegetated steep terrain came as the Grand Canyon region – and the Colorado River basin that runs through it – continue to be mired in a severe drought that has fueled a widespread water crisis.
Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions. The sudden and strong rainstorm that fueled this catastrophic flood may have been been supercharged by the historic El Niño that has sharply increased sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, which has the ability to affect weather systems around the world.

Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say


Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’




The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.
UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.

With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.
Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”


Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused on plastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.
Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.
Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”
She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping

The datacentre power spat highlights a hidden truth: we’re not building renewables fast enough to meet our needs

Alison Reeve





A battle over datacentre power sources is only part of the picture. Australia needs a much bigger electricity system to meet all future demand





Anthony Albanese has been clear that he wants a set of national standards to ensure datacentre growth accelerates Australia’s push to renewables and keeps a lid on power prices. At the centre of his desired policies was a “BYO power” requirement – a condition that all new datacentres would be powered by 100% renewable electricity.
But last week these aims collided with the Queensland and Northern Territory governments’ desire to rely on their state-owned gas and coal power stations to power datacentres.

As a result, we got a national cabinet communique that was carefully worded to allow every first minister to claim a win, but little clarity about what rules would apply.
On Friday, the energy minister, Chris Bowen, reiterated the federal government’s intent to legislate binding national standards for datacentres across the country which will require them to use 100% renewables, backed by firming – which can be gas.
The potential for a carve-out is still there, with Bowen saying the federal government would consider concessions – but only if state-owned generation can provide a cheaper power mix.






What will we get out of the AI boom? The data suggests lots of noisy, energy-hungry datacentres and not much else 
Greg Jericho


Read more
At first glance, this looks unlikely. Electricity costs are about 10% of total expenditure for a datacentre. Gas is the most expensive form of generation, and new coal is more expensive than new renewables. Even existing coal gets undercut by cheap solar for much of the day. Existing centres are already choosing to run on about 70% renewable electricity, through a power purchase agreement with a wind or solar farm, because they want to keep their costs down.
Using gas and coal power (as Queensland and the NT are pushing for) would probably increase electricity costs for datacentres. It would also probably delay their development, because the waitlist to receive new gas turbines is years-long.
In any case, the energy source for potential new datacentres is only one part of the picture.

articles.title: 7 common heat pump myths – and the truth behind them
articles.raw_rss: From fears about cold weather and noise to concerns over cost and disruptive installations, heat pumps are still surrounded by misconceptions. We separate the myths from the facts

SPONSORED BY OCTOPUS ENERGY

The Independent Home Channel is powered by Octopus Energy.
Heat pumps are fast becoming one of the most talked-about, low-carbon alternatives to gas boilers in UK homes. Very simply, they work by extracting heat from the air or ground outside and using it to warm your home and hot water. Unlike a boiler, where the temperature can yo-yo, a heat pump will keep your home at a constant temperature and running costs can be lower. 
As interest grows, companies such as Octopus Energy have played a role in bringing heat pumps into the mainstream, offering installation services for homeowners looking to switch. But despite their rising popularity, heat pumps are still widely misunderstood. From concerns about cold weather performance to expensive installation, a number of myths continue to circulate. Here are some of the common misconceptions and the reality behind them.

Recommended

Do solar panels add value to a house? How they affect property prices
Using solar panels with your heat pump can reduce bills – here’s how
ECO4 grant eligibility: How to apply for free UK solar panels

“Heat pumps don’t work in cold weather”
Not true. Heat pumps are designed to extract heat from the air even when temperatures drop as low as -20C. 





Admittedly, on the rare days it does get cold in the UK, a heat pump will need to work harder and use more electricity to capture and compress that heat. However, it still delivers more heat energy than the electricity it consumes. A heat pump typically produces around three to four units of heat for every one unit of electricity used. 
By comparison, a gas boiler generates heat by burning fuel, with some energy lost through combustion and flue gases and typically operates at around 85 to 95 per cent efficiency. 

“Heat pumps have to be on south-facing walls”
A myth. Heat pumps can in fact be installed on any external wall, provided there is enough space and airflow around the unit. Other factors such as pipe runs, noise considerations and access for maintenance are far more important than the direction the unit faces.

“Heat pumps can replace air conditioning in heatwaves”
Yes, and no; it depends on the type of heat pump you have. Most heat pumps installed in UK homes are air-to-water systems; some models can offer cooling as well as heating, but it is not a standard feature.


If you're looking for both heating and air conditioning, an air-to-air heat pump is the better option, although they are less commonly fitted in the UK. If cooling is a priority, it's worth discussing the best heat pump for your home with your installer.

Andy Burnham should call a cross-party meeting to discuss the UK’s response to worsening extreme weather, including the forthcoming ‘super El Niño’, the Liberal Democrats have said.
The prime minister chaired a Cobra emergency meeting on the drought earlier this month but there has been little from the government on the wider threats posed by five successive heatwaves since May and expected global issues with food shortages and inflation.

Pippa Heylings, the Lib Dem spokesperson for energy security and net zero, said: “Andy Burnham has shown he is able to commit to talking about things people care about, which is good. But there’s been a baffling silence from him on extreme heat. What we have heard so far has been underwhelming. Banning disposable barbecues is good, but we need to see more.”


Heylings and Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, wrote to Burnham a fortnight ago, proposing a meeting of the UK’s party leaders “to discuss the long-term measures needed to protect our country from climate impacts and build resilience to the extreme weather we are already experiencing”. They say they have not had a response.
Heylings contrasted Burnham’s reluctance to address the climate crisis with his prioritising of social care, on which he has called for cross-party support: “We want the same approach [to the climate].”
She said even the leaders of Reform and the Conservatives, both of whom have vowed to scrap net zero and downplayed the climate crisis, should be able to join in an effort to protect the UK. “I think there is not a single MP who would not want to show their constituents they were trying to prepare us [for the impacts of extreme weather],” she said.
The forthcoming El Niño could bring more serious problems, Heylings said. “The scale of this Super El Niño is unprecedented and will have impacts here in the UK exacerbating our extreme weather particularly with more intense flooding and storms over the autumn and winter. We’re looking at a double whammy.”
Any cross-party approach should not be limited to discussing preparedness for extreme weather, she said. “The key question is how do we stop it worsening?”

It’s hard to believe that a mountain range as mighty as the Himalayas can actually be fragile and increasingly unstable, but the avalanches, landslides and floods that have always shaped and scoured the valleys are now in overdrive as temperatures rise twice as fast in Nepal as the global average.



Hotter conditions mean that the ice that acts as a glue to bind the rocks is now melting. Giant glaciers are being diminished and weakened, and frozen soil, known as permafrost, is thawing.





The result is that a region home to important shrines for Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims and popular destinations for climbers and trekkers is becoming more volatile. 



Inevitably, this raises questions about whether it’s possible for the Nepalese to live safely in a landscape that’s sacred but unpredictable – and how to advise visitors about when, or even whether, they should go.

A massive chunk of ice and rock crashed into the valley below with enough force to set off earthquake alarms. That created a tsunami of water, mud and debris, which surged down a string of valleys known as the Bhoti Koshi-Trishuli corridor, tearing bridges and buildings from their foundations.

Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, will replace Mr Griffith as shadow business secretary, while Sir Mel will join Tory big beasts Dame Priti Patel and Sir James Cleverly on the backbenches amid the ongoing shake-up.
A Reform UK spokesman said: "Kemi is simply moving the deckchairs around the titanic with this reshuffle. She has promoted ardent supporters of net zero and the ECHR into senior positions, despite saying she wouldn’t .
"The Conservatives haven’t learned a thing from their failures in office."

Meanwhile, Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper also slammed the Tories for a "race to the bottom" with Mr Farage's party. 
The Chelmsford MP and the party's Treasury spokeswoman said: "[Mr Griffith] helped deliver the Truss mini-budget that sent mortgages soaring and the economy into turmoil. 
"It’s clear Conservatives haven't learned a thing. His appt to Shadow Chancellor shows they're happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility in their race to the bottom with Reform UK."

Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global supplies


Organisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflict




Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food.
Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation of Bhutan for the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists.

Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.”
Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.”


View image in fullscreen
Tshering Tobgay: ‘Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices.’ Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks


Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas




Turkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.
Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.

The Guardian revealed in 2023 that Turkmenistan was the worst country for methane mega-leaks. Sources in Turkmenistan said this scrutiny was the “critical step” in leading the secretive and authoritarian government to engage with foreign partners.
A “super-emitter” leak, the escape of tonnes of methane per hour from a single valve or pipeline, heats the planet more than the emissions from a million SUVs or an entire coal-fired power station.
Turkmenistan had now stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The work was an “incredible first step”, said the UN, but much remained to be done.


View image in fullscreen
A satellite image of a methane leak in Turkmenistan’s Lebap province, which was plugged in March after a corroded pipe was fixed. Illustration: UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory


The UN Methane Alert and Response System (Mars) sent 192 alerts of methane plumes to Turkmenistan in the last year. The country had three of the six worst leaks detected in the world by Mars in last six months, and nine of the top 50.
Turkmenistan responded to about 20% of the alerts with on-the-ground information about the leaks and potential plans to fix them. In contrast, the US was sent the second highest number of alerts – 138 – but responded to none and had fixed no leaks in the last year. Other nations that failed to respond to any alerts were Iran, Russia and China.

The worst methane leak detected was an extraordinary leak in Mexico’s offshore oil and gas industry of 37 tonnes per hour, equivalent to the emissions of more than 7m SUVs. Mexico responded to all 23 Mars alerts in the last year, but had yet to complete a fix.

Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.

Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible

Wesley Morgan for the Conversation





Climate change is the greatest threat to the Pacific, with fuel shortages and missile tests also on the agenda as Anthony Albanese heads to Palau





Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda.
China is testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies.

And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.
But the forum will be missing key leaders – Solomon Islands’ prime minister, Matthew Wale, made a shock departure, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.

Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. As president of negotiations of the Cop31 climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline.
China’s missile test
Since the second world war, the United States has maintained fortified bases in the Pacific and an unrivalled deep-water navy (the US also regularly tests long-range missiles in the region). However, China’s investment in military capabilities has challenged the status quo.
In July, China launched a nuclear-capable test missile that flew over multiple Pacific nations and hit waters close to Tuvalu’s exclusive economic zone.

The Guardian view on rare earths: it’s common sense to secure essential supply chains

Editorial





Outsourcing the industry to China cannot continue, but Europe knows it can no longer count on the US for a solution





The alarm sounded 16 years ago. In 2010, China blocked exports of key rare earths to Japan in a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea. The critical minerals are essential to everything from advanced weaponry and iPhones to electric vehicle batteries and wind turbines, so the rest of the world took note. But it didn’t take much action. China still accounts for about 70% of rare-earth mining globally and 90% of separation and processing.
Then, last year, Beijing forced Donald Trump to back away from his trade war – not with its retaliatory tariffs, but the curbing of rare-earth exports. A scramble for new supplies began in earnest. The year-long trade truce is due to expire in November. The price of erbium, an element essential to communications infrastructure, has already jumped because of fears that export controls will soon be renewed.



The 17 metals known as rare earths are far from rare; their name refers to the low concentrations in which they are found. Extraction and processing are costly, complex and often dirty, while returns are low. That’s why the US – which dominated the industry in the 1980s – and others outsourced production to China. Any plan to diversify supply chains must somehow build in predictable demand and pricing to succeed. Even now, US rare earths are reportedly flowing to Asia because of the lack of domestic demand. While “Big shovel” is becoming the new driver of geopolitics, rare earths are a tiny slice of the critical minerals market – worth less than $6bn globally last year.
Efforts to diversify supply chains had already begun. But the US-China standoff accelerated them. Last autumn, the Pentagon became the single largest investor in the US firm MP Minerals. In February, the Trump administration announced that it would spend $12bn to create a critical minerals reserve, focusing initially on rare earths. US officials have reportedly described their plan to create new supply chains as a “Manhattan Project” for rare earths. Others question the strategy behind the splurge of money and projects.
China, which imports rare earths for processing and has seen them affected by the war in Myanmar, also wants to diversify its supplies. articles.title: Hero teacher saved over 1,600 children from Nepal floods as death toll exceeds 700
articles.raw_rss:
A hero teacher saved over 1,600 children from the Nepal floods as the death toll now exceeds 700 people.Rajendra Dadabi, head teacher at Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, a three-storey school in the Trishuli valley of north-central Nepal, made the heroic call to evacuate classrooms after being informed by a friend five miles upstream that their town village had been devastated by the flash flooding that took place on Wednesday. Mr Dabadi said he received a panicked call from a friend: “He said the village was gone: taken by the river. He told me to run.”The 47-year-old teacher knew that the school was 60 metres above the river and was structurally strong as it was built from concrete, and was the same height as the bridge that linked the village to the east bank of the river.

articles.jina_text:
People have been warned to stay away from a popular beauty spot pond used for swimming and other water sports due to "hidden hazards" exposed by reduced water levels.
Keepers Pond in Abergavenny poses "serious safety risks" with levels dangerously low, according to Bannau Brycheiniog National Park, also known as the Brecon Beacons.
It said that along with the prolonged dry spell, the water had been used to tackle recent wildfires.
"As the water has receded, previously hidden hazards and unknown objects have been exposed on the pond bed, creating serious safety risks. For your own safety, you must not enter the water under any circumstances," the park authority said in a Facebook post.

Getty Images
Keepers Pond (pictured in 2020) is ordinarily a popular spot for swimming and water sports
The restriction applies to all activities on or in the water, including swimming, paddleboarding, kayaking, and any other water-based activities.
"We ask that visitors respect the area and do not remove, disturb or interfere with any objects or features revealed by the low water levels," it said.
The beauty spot car park remains open to visitors but "for your own safety", the national park said, "you must not enter the water under any circumstances".

articles.summary: Swimmers and water sports enthusiasts have been warned to avoid Keepers Pond in Abergavenny after drought and wildfire-fighting efforts caused water levels to drop dangerously low. The reduced levels have exposed previously hidden hazards and unknown objects on the pond bed, creating serious safety risks. The ban covers all water-based activities including swimming, paddleboarding, and kayaking, amid Wales-wide drought conditions linked to record-low river levels and widespread wildfires.

articles.title: Where thunderstorms and flooding will hit UK – and when heatwave could return
articles.raw_rss: Festivals and sporting events could be disrupted over the bank holiday weekend as the Met Office warns of heavy rain
articles.raw_content:
Thunderstorms are set to hit parts of southern England and Wales on Saturday, with heavy rain likely to disrupt festivals and other bank holiday weekend events.



The Met Office has issued a yellow weather warning stretching from south-west England and parts of Wales across the Midlands to eastern England. The warning will be in force from midday until 9pm on Saturday.



The forecaster warned of a risk of flash flooding after an unusually dry summer, with travellers told to expect longer journey times as the rain sets in for the weekend, with England, Wales and Northern Ireland observing a bank holiday on Monday.





Where are thunderstorms forecast?



The Met Office said Saturday will be a “very unsettled day for England and Wales”, with “thunderstorms, lightning, hail by later in the afternoon”. 



Met Office meteorologist Greg Dewhurst told The i Paper that those in the affected area could face “really heavy rain” for the rest of the day into Sunday.



“Some places could see an inch of rain in less than an hour,” Dewhurst said. “This is likely to lead to surface flooding, it could lead to some surface water on the roads.”



He also warned that while places within the yellow warning zone will experience the “most intense” rainfall, other areas are going to be very wet this weekend, with heavy rain expected from the west of England to Wales and Northern Ireland on Saturday.



A yellow weather warning is in place across central and southern parts of England and Wales

Where are thunderstorms forecast? 
The Met Office said Saturday will be a “very unsettled day for England and Wales”, with “thunderstorms, lightning, hail by later in the afternoon”.  
Met Office meteorologist Greg Dewhurst told The i Paper that those in the affected area could face “really heavy rain” for the rest of the day into Sunday. 
“Some places could see an inch of rain in less than an hour,” Dewhurst said. “This is likely to lead to surface flooding, it could lead to some surface water on the roads.” 
He also warned that while places within the yellow warning zone will experience the “most intense” rainfall, other areas are going to be very wet this weekend, with heavy rain expected from the west of England to Wales and Northern Ireland on Saturday.



 

A yellow weather warning is in place across central and southern parts of England and Wales (Photo: Met Office) 
There is also an increased risk of surface flooding in England and Wales, where the drought has left the ground dry and unable to absorb water quickly. The Met Office previously said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record after five heatwaves. 
“Really hard, dry ground and then intense rainfall means the rain can’t seep through the ground,” Dewhurst said.  
Scotland and the north of England will have a “muggy feel” on Saturday, whilst in southern England, temperatures will drop to around 22°C. 
Will events be cancelled?  
Rain delayed the start of play at Lord’s cricket ground on the third day of the second men’s Test match between England and Pakistan. 
“Rainfall and cricket don’t go well together,” said Dewhurst. “We can expect highly reduced play today with rain going through.” 
While he expects “some disruption” to smaller local events like village fetes, Dewhurst thinks larger music festivals in Reading and Leeds will go ahead as planned, though he recommended festival-goers prepare for their “muddy clothes”. 

Ground staff wipe water the play surface at Lord’s cricket ground as play gets delayed by rain (Photo: Dave Shopland/AP) 
Will the weather improve over the weekend? 
Dewhurst said the area of low pressure bringing the rain will pull away tonight, with rainfall easing off, but another weather front moving in on Sunday means Saturday’s weather is likely to be repeated.
